sentences.text: The name Coelurus translates to "hollow tail," a reference to the animal's possession of hollow tail vertebrae.
This creature was a small, bipedal carnivore equipped with long legs.
Estimates suggest the animal weighed between 13 and 20 kilograms, measured about 2.4 meters in length, and stood 0.7 meters tall at the hip.
Reconstructions indicate it featured a long neck and torso, long slender hindlimbs, and a potentially small, slender skull.
The only valid species of Coelurus is C. fragilis, which was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879.
Fossil evidence comes from a single partial skeleton discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, United States.
The main skeleton of Coelurus is nearly complete and is currently housed at the Peabody Museum of Natural History.
Coelurus was a small terrestrial carnivore that fed on small prey such as insects, mammals, and lizards.

Since the 1980s, Coelurus has generally been classified as a coelurosaurian with uncertain affinities that does not fit well into better-known Cretaceous clades, though it is also described as a ceratosaurian dinosaur.
Coelurus belongs to the parent group Coelurosauria.
Coelurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically between 155 and 152 million years ago.
It is debated whether Coelurus groups with compsognathids, as Oliver Rauhut proposed in 2003 but later studies failed to support.

There is a debate over whether Coelurus is a tyrannosauroid or a basal coelurosaur; Senter proposed it was a tyrannosauroid, but Turner et al. found it to be a basal coelurosaur more derived than tyrannosaurids.
Some researchers interpret a Late Jurassic theropod vertebra formerly referred to Coelurus fragilis, along with a theropod astragalus and Calamosaurus foxi, as alvarezsauroids.
